The third UN Water Conference will take place in Abu Dhabi from 8 to 10 December 2026. It will provide an opportunity for researchers, practitioners and policymakers to exchange perspectives and develop shared solutions to the challenges posed by water insecurity. More broadly, the conference should encourage the entire community of water stakeholders to reflect critically on the strengths and weaknesses of the water agenda, understood as the set of goals, policies and actions intended to manage, protect and equitably share freshwater resources, and to consider how it must evolve to become more effective. Aerial view of an oasis in Al Ain, Abu Dhabi. Credit: Stefan Tomic/E+/Getty Traditional approaches to water-related challenges have arguably been shaped by the assumption that wealthy countries should develop technologies and effective governance models, and then transfer these solutions to poorer countries. Numerous experts have highlighted the limitations of this approach, which, despite often being well intentioned, can be both patronizing and paternalistic. Yet the mainstream discourse has changed little. The Comment by Mabhaudhi and colleagues illustrates what can be overlooked when water challenges are viewed through this top-down lens. Africa is commonly associated with water scarcity and water-related diseases. Although these challenges are undeniable, communities across the continent have extensive experience of living with water uncertainty. Their responses draw on scientific and Indigenous knowledge, the interplay between technology and governance, and the participation of affected communities in decision-making. Recognizing and learning from this experience would challenge the assumption that knowledge and solutions flow primarily from wealthy countries to poorer ones. At the beginning of 2026, Nature Water partnered with UN-Water to commission a series of Comments highlighting topics often overlooked in mainstream discussions about water and proposing actions to help shape the future of the water agenda. The resulting contributions are now brought together in the online collection, Transforming the Water Agenda . Together with the articles in the companion Focus in Nature Sustainability , these contributions are intended to stimulate discussion and support the continued development of the water agenda at the UN Water Conference and beyond. The Comment by Mabhaudhi and colleagues provides one example of the perspectives represented in the collection. Other contributions approach the water agenda from distinct angles, but several common themes transpire. One of the strongest messages to emerge is that technological advances are essential, but insufficient on their own. Water security also depends on empowering the people and communities that manage water resources and equipping them with the necessary knowledge and skills. For example, the growing availability of water data could drive substantial progress, but it also risks widening inequalities between rich and poor. Data must therefore be made broadly accessible so that people across different demographic groups can use them to improve water governance 1 . Similarly, investments in technology and infrastructure will achieve little unless accompanied by efforts to train people to operate and maintain new systems 2 . Infrastructure planning must also account for an ageing population and a potentially shrinking water workforce 3 . More fundamentally, approaches to water security remain too focused on assigning responsibility after harm has occurred, whether because of water scarcity or extreme weather. Instead, they should recognize the human right to water and prioritize the early identification of risks to prevent harm (see the Comment by Müller and colleagues). The need to move from reaction to anticipation is echoed elsewhere in the collection. Substantial effort is devoted to understanding and describing water crises after they occur. Although this work is essential to preventing similar crises in the future, the prevailing mindset remains too focused on learning from the past rather than generating actionable foresight (see Comment by AghaKouchak and colleagues). Financial systems must undergo a similar shift, moving away from primarily funding recovery after losses and towards investing in adaptation and resilience before crises occur 4 . More broadly, the scientific community should move beyond reacting to political decisions and take a more active role in setting the agenda 5 . Underlying these arguments is a broader need to place water at the centre of the global agenda. Rather than being treated as secondary to other major societal challenges, water should be recognized as the medium through which many of them become visible and can be addressed.
